```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(rscprep)
library(Seurat)
```

`seuratFrom10x()` hands back a named list -- one Seurat object per sample.
`mergeSeurat()` is the other half of that pairing: it collapses the list into
a single object you can take through a normalisation and integration
workflow, without losing track of which cell came from which sample.

```{r, child = "_heart1k.Rmd"}
```

```{r, child = "_pseudo-samples.Rmd"}
```

## The basic pipeline

With real data, the list comes straight from `seuratFrom10x()`:

```{r pipeline-real, eval = FALSE}
seurat_list <- seuratFrom10x(
  path  = "/path/to/Pool1/outs",
  multi = TRUE
)
```

Here it is the pseudo-sample list built above, and the merge is the same
either way:

```{r pipeline}
merged <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)
```

That is the whole intended usage: the list `seuratFrom10x()` returns is
already in the shape `mergeSeurat()` expects, so nothing needs renaming or
reordering in between.

## What the list names are for

The names of `objList` are not decoration -- they are passed to `merge()` as
`add.cell.id`, so each becomes a prefix on that sample's cell barcodes:

```{r barcodes}
colnames(seurat_list$Sample_A)[1:2]

colnames(merged)[1:2]
```

This matters because 10x barcodes are drawn from a fixed whitelist, so the
same barcode routinely appears in several samples. Prefixing keeps them
distinct and keeps every cell traceable back to its origin. It is also why
names must be present and unique -- `mergeSeurat()` refuses to merge a list
that is unnamed, has blank or `NA` names, or repeats a name.

The `Ident` column set by `seuratFrom10x()` is carried through the merge, so
you can still split or group by sample afterwards:

```{r idents}
table(merged$Ident)
```

## What gets checked

The list is validated before anything is merged, so a bad batch fails with a
message naming the offending sample rather than producing a subtly wrong
object. `mergeSeurat()` requires that `objList`:

* is non-empty;
* contains only structurally valid Seurat objects;
* is fully named, with no blank, `NA` or duplicated names;
* contains no zero-cell objects;
* agrees on `DefaultAssay()` across every element.

```{r duplicated-names, error = TRUE}
mergeSeurat(setNames(seurat_list, c("Sample_A", "Sample_A", "Sample_C")))
```

The assay check is about *agreement*, not about `RNA` specifically -- a list
of `ADT` objects merges fine, a list mixing `RNA` and `ADT` does not.

Two more checks run after the merge, to catch a merge that silently lost
data: every sample must still be present in the merged `Ident` column, and
the merged cell count must equal the sum of the inputs'.

## Two behaviours worth knowing

A single-element list short-circuits. The lone object is returned as-is,
with a message -- unmerged, and with its barcodes left unprefixed:

```{r single}
one <- seuratFrom10x(path = outs, multi = FALSE)

merged_one <- mergeSeurat(one)
colnames(merged_one)[1:2]
```

And the merged object is returned **invisibly**, after being printed. So a
bare call shows you the result without flooding the console twice, but you
still need to assign it to keep it:

```{r invisible, eval = FALSE}
mergeSeurat(seurat_list)             # prints a summary; result is not kept
merged <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)   # assign to keep it
```

## Seurat 4 and Seurat 5

`mergeSeurat()` detects which Seurat is installed. Under Seurat 4, `merge()`
binds every sample's counts into one matrix. Under Seurat 5 it keeps one
layer per sample instead (`counts.Sample_A`, `counts.Sample_B`, ...).
`mergeSeurat()` joins those layers by default, so the merged object has the
same shape under either version and code downstream does not need to know
which one made it.

Seurat 5's own integration workflow, `IntegrateLayers()`, wants the layers
split. Ask for that with `joinLayers = FALSE`; under Seurat 4 the argument
does nothing:

```{r split-layers, eval = FALSE}
merged <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list, joinLayers = FALSE)
```
